presenceLabel: Kickapoo village or claim in this area
presenceNote: Kickapoo lived in Indiana and Illinois from the 1730s–40s (Indiana DNR; Wikipedia’s account of where they were at first contact differs, so no single location is asserted) and have no documented village in Kentucky. The nation is shown c.1730s–1819 (low–medium confidence). The Mascouten merged into the Kickapoo and have no area of their own: their story is shown on this page, at very low confidence, with no separate town located. The Kickapoo frontier story is shown as c.1775–1795 (Revolution to Greenville); the sources date Kickapoo events only at 1791 (Scott), 1795, 1805, 1809 and 1819.
overlapNote: Shared the Wabash with the Mascouten (who merged with them), Wea, Piankashaw, Miami and later Potawatomi. The 1819 treaty says part of the land was taken 'by conquest from the Illinois nation'. Kickapoo were not at the 1805 Grouseland treaty, which left their Vermillion claim alone.
basis: Treaty texts (Grouseland 1805, Edwardsville 1819), Scott's 1791 report, Indiana DNR. Wikipedia (Kickapoo people) used only for background, and it does not mention Kentucky or the Revolution.

eras.label: 1730s–1791 · Kickapoo and Mascouten on the Wabash
eras.text: Indiana DNR has the Kickapoo, closely tied to the Mascouten, moving from Illinois into north-west and west-central Indiana in the 1730s–40s and living along the Wabash and its tributaries. Wikipedia instead puts them in northern Ohio or on the southern Wabash near Terre Haute at first contact. The sources disagree, and the map does not choose between them. The Mascouten (the “Fire Nation” of the Jesuit accounts) united with the Kickapoo and Meskwaki in 1712 and were last named as a band in 1779 on the Wabash; later records count them as part of the Kickapoo. No separate Mascouten town is located, so they have no area of their own: confidence for them is very low. No Kickapoo village in Kentucky is documented. The tint is an approximate general area built from whole counties (the three counties the sources name, widened to their neighbours), not a boundary.

eras.label: 1791 · Scott and Wilkinson on the Wabash
eras.text: In 1791 Scott’s Kentucky volunteers attacked a Kickapoo town opposite the Wea villages near Ouiatenon, and Hardin’s detachment took 52 prisoners on 1 June. Scott’s report names Kickapoo and Wea towns; it does not name the Mascouten, who by then were counted with the Kickapoo, so no separate Mascouten place is shown.

eras.label: 1792–1805 · Statehood, Greenville, Grouseland
eras.text: Kickapoo are named in the Greenville preamble and annuity list (1795); in 1805 the Grouseland treaty reserved the Kickapoo claim to the Vermillion River country (the tinted general area, approximate). None of the sources shows Kickapoo claiming Kentucky hunting rights in 1792.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · Kentucky: none documented

eras.label: 1809–1819 · Cessions
eras.text: 9 Dec 1809 (Vincennes) and 30 Jul 1819 (Edwardsville): the Kickapoo ceded Wabash and Illinois lands, claiming part ‘by descent’ and the rest ‘by conquest from the Illinois nation’ and possession ‘for more than half a century’. The 1819 line has unlocated corners (the upper point of the 1809 cession), so it is text only.
